cards.title: Domain Events: Facts, Not Commands
cards.teaser: A domain event is a record of something that happened in the domain — a fact, already past, already true. It cannot be rejected. It cannot be undone. It is the domain's way of saying: this occurred.

runs.text: Vaughn Vernon, in
Implementing Domain-Driven Design

(2013), defines a domain event as "something that happened in the domain that domain experts care about." The definition contains two requirements: it must have happened (past tense, immutable), and it must matter to the business.
Domain events capture
significant state transitions

in the domain. Not every state change warrants an event — only those that carry business meaning. A counter incrementing in a cache does not warrant an event. An order moving from "pending" to "confirmed" does.

items.text: Past tense
— events describe what happened, not what should happen. They are immutable records.
Undeniable
— events cannot be rejected by handlers. A handler may fail to process an event, but the event itself already occurred.
Domain-meaningful
— the event uses ubiquitous language. It is legible to domain experts, not just developers.
Lightweight carrier
— an event carries just enough information for handlers to act on. It is not a database row dump.

runs.text: Eric Evans introduced domain events as a tactical pattern in the 2010 addendum to Domain-Driven Design. Vernon's IDDD gave the pattern its full treatment, making it central to aggregate design and context integration.
A domain event is a business-meaningful fact that already happened — like a receipt. You can't cancel a receipt; you can only issue a refund, which is a new event.

cards.title: Naming Domain Events: Past-Tense Ubiquitous Language
cards.teaser: Domain events are named in the past tense using the same ubiquitous language the business uses. OrderPlaced, PaymentReceived, ShipmentDispatched — the name alone should tell a domain expert what happened, when, and why it matters.

runs.text: Event naming is not a technical decision — it is a modeling decision. The name encodes business intent and belongs to the bounded context's ubiquitous language. A name that requires a comment to explain what it means is a poorly-chosen name.
Rules for naming domain events:

items.text: Past tense, always.
OrderPlaced, not PlaceOrder. PaymentReceived, not ReceivePayment. The past tense signals that the event records history, not intent.
Domain vocabulary, not technical vocabulary.
OrderStatusUpdated is a weak event name — it is a database description. OrderPlaced, OrderCancelled, and OrderFulfilled are strong — they are domain descriptions.
Specific enough to be unambiguous.
ItemAddedToCart is better than CartChanged. PaymentFailed is better than PaymentProcessed with a status field.
Use the same noun the domain uses for the aggregate.
If the bounded context calls it a "Subscription", the event is SubscriptionActivated, not AccountActivated — even if both describe the same underlying record.

runs.text: Common naming patterns by domain context:

items.text: Order context:
OrderPlaced, OrderConfirmed, OrderShipped, OrderCancelled, OrderRefunded
Payments context:
PaymentAuthorized, PaymentCaptured, PaymentFailed, RefundIssued
Inventory context:
StockReserved, StockReplenished, StockDepleted, ReservationExpired

runs.text: Name events the way a domain expert would describe what happened in a business meeting — past tense, specific, no technical jargon. If the name makes sense in a status report to a stakeholder, it is probably right.

cards.title: Event Payload: Minimal vs Rich
cards.teaser: What an event carries matters as much as what it is named. Too little and handlers must query back; too much and events become fragile contracts that break whenever the source model changes. The right payload is a deliberate design decision.

runs.text: Two payload strategies exist, each with trade-offs:

items.text: Thin (notification) payload
— the event carries only the identity of the changed aggregate and the event type. Handlers that need detail query the source. Example:
{ eventType: "OrderPlaced", orderId: "ord-123", occurredAt: "2024-01-15T10:00:00Z" }
. Simple, stable, but requires a round-trip to fetch details.
Rich (self-contained) payload

— the event carries everything handlers are likely to need, reducing or eliminating follow-up queries. Example: includes order total, customer ID, line items, and shipping address. Eliminates coupling to a query API but increases event size and the risk of over-sharing private aggregate state.

runs.text: Factors that should drive the choice:

items.text: Handler latency requirements.
If handlers must respond in milliseconds, round-trips to query the source are expensive. Rich payloads are justified.
Bounded context boundaries.
Cross-context consumers often cannot query the source directly. They need the event to be self-contained.
Aggregate privacy.
Some aggregate fields are internal. Publishing them in events leaks private model details. Include only what is part of the published language.
Event sourcing.
If events are the primary state store, payload must be rich enough to reconstruct state from events alone. No round-trips are possible.

runs.text: A common pragmatic rule: for intra-context domain events, lean thin. For integration events crossing context boundaries, lean rich. Cross-context consumers cannot be expected to query back into a foreign context.

A thin event is like a text notification: "your package shipped, see tracking link." A rich event is like an email with all order details embedded. Thin is simpler to produce; rich is more useful for consumers who can't follow the link.

cards.title: When to Raise Events: Significant State Transitions
cards.teaser: Not every change raises an event — only transitions that carry business meaning. The discipline of choosing when to raise events forces explicit modeling of what matters in the domain and what the domain needs other parts of the system to know about.

runs.text: Domain events should be raised at
significant state transitions

— moments in the aggregate lifecycle that domain experts recognize as important. The test: would a domain expert say "yes, that happened" when reviewing the event? If so, it belongs. If not, it is an implementation detail.
Transitions that typically warrant events:

items.text: Lifecycle inflection points.
Creation, activation, suspension, cancellation, completion. These are the business state machine transitions that define what the aggregate is at any given moment.
External commitments.
When the domain makes a promise to the outside world — a reservation is confirmed, a payment is authorized — that promise crossing the boundary is event-worthy.
Policy triggers.
When a rule fires that will trigger downstream behavior — an overdue invoice triggers a late fee, an inventory level hitting zero triggers a reorder.
Transitions with audit value.
Any change where the business might later ask "when did that happen, and under what conditions?" deserves an event.

runs.text: What should NOT raise events:

items.text: Internal bookkeeping that has no business meaning (a counter incrementing, a flag toggling).
Read operations — querying the domain never produces an event.
Implementation-level state that maps to no domain concept.

runs.text: Raise an event when a domain expert would write "and then the order was placed" in a business scenario. Skip it when you'd write "and then the database row was updated" — that's an implementation detail, not a domain event.

cards.title: Event Publication Patterns: Collect on Aggregate, Publish Post-Commit
cards.teaser: Aggregates do not publish events directly — they collect events internally during a transaction. The application service publishes those collected events after the transaction commits. This two-phase pattern ensures events are only published for state changes that actually persisted.

runs.text: Raising an event inside the aggregate during a domain operation, then immediately publishing it, creates a dangerous race condition: the event could be delivered before the aggregate's state change is committed to the database. Handlers would then react to an event for a change that may not persist.
The correct two-phase pattern:

items.text: Phase 1 — Collect.
The aggregate appends events to an internal collection during the domain operation. Events are not published yet. The aggregate is saved to the database in the same transaction.
Phase 2 — Publish.
After the transaction commits successfully, the application service reads the collected events from the aggregate and dispatches them to the event bus or domain event dispatcher.

runs.text: A canonical aggregate implementation in C#:

Publishing events before committing the transaction is a subtle but serious bug. If the commit fails after publication, handlers will have reacted to an event for a change that never happened. Always commit first, publish second.

The aggregate is a notepad — it writes down what happened as it happens. The application service only announces what's on the notepad after the transaction succeeds. You only send the announcement once you're sure the change actually stuck.

cards.title: Domain Events vs Integration Events
cards.teaser: Domain events are internal signals within a bounded context. Integration events cross context boundaries and act as published contracts between separate subsystems. They look similar but serve different masters, have different payload conventions, and evolve under different rules.

runs.text: The distinction between domain events and integration events is one of the most practically important in event-driven DDD. Confusing the two leads to either over-coupling between contexts or under-specified inter-context contracts.

items.text: Domain events

are intra-context. They fire within the same bounded context, typically within the same process or transaction boundary. They use the context's own ubiquitous language. They are consumed by domain event handlers in the same context. They may be ephemeral — they do not need to survive process restarts.
Integration events

cross context boundaries, often crossing process boundaries via a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus). They form the published language between contexts. They must survive broker failures. Their schema is a public contract that must be versioned.

runs.text: The typical flow: a domain event fires inside Context A, an event handler in Context A translates it into an integration event with a stable, cross-context schema, and publishes it to the message broker. Context B subscribes to the integration event and responds using its own internal domain events.
Key differences at a glance:

items.text: Scope:
domain = one context; integration = multiple contexts.
Language:
domain = rich internal model; integration = shared/published language.
Durability:
domain = may be in-memory; integration = must persist to a broker.
Versioning:
domain = context-local; integration = semver contracts managed across teams.

runs.text: Domain events are like internal memos — they stay inside the department. Integration events are like press releases — they go out to other departments and must be carefully worded because you can't take them back.

cards.title: Domain Events vs Commands: Past vs Imperative
cards.teaser: Commands say "please do this" — they can be rejected. Events say "this happened" — they cannot. The distinction shapes whether a subscriber has authority to refuse, whether the sender cares about the outcome, and how failures propagate across the system.

runs.text: Commands and events are the two primary message types in DDD messaging, and they are intentionally different in semantics:

items.text: Command

— imperative, directed. PlaceOrder, CancelShipment, AuthorizePayment. A command requests that something be done. It is sent to exactly one handler. That handler may reject it — validation fails, business rules are violated, preconditions are not met. The sender typically awaits confirmation or failure.
Event

— declarative, broadcast. OrderPlaced, ShipmentCancelled, PaymentAuthorized. An event announces that something occurred. It is published to zero or more handlers. Handlers cannot reject it. The publisher does not know or care who is listening.

runs.text: The table below summarizes the distinction:

items.text: Tense:
command = imperative (PlaceOrder); event = past tense (OrderPlaced).
Addressee:
command = one handler; event = zero or many handlers.
Rejection:
command = can be rejected; event = cannot be rejected.
Sender awareness:
command = sender awaits result; event = publisher fire-and-forget.
Direction:
command = intent (future); event = record (past).

runs.text: In Event Storming (Alberto Brandolini's collaborative modeling technique), commands and events are color-coded: blue for commands, orange for events. The flow is: command fires, aggregate processes it, event is produced. Modeling in this sequence makes the causal chain explicit.
A command is a request that can be turned down. An event is a notification that cannot — it already happened. You send commands to get things done; you listen to events to learn what has been done.

cards.title: Event Handlers: Intra-Context and Cross-Context
cards.teaser: An event handler is any component that reacts to a domain event. Intra-context handlers live in the same bounded context and can access the same domain model. Cross-context handlers translate integration events into actions in a foreign context — and must do so without assuming shared state.

runs.text: Event handlers are the consumers of events. Their design depends entirely on whether they are in the same bounded context as the publisher or in a separate one.
Intra-context handlers:

items.text: Run synchronously (or near-synchronously) in the same process, often in the same transaction or immediately after it.
Can access the same domain model, repositories, and services as the event publisher.

Typical responsibilities: triggering a secondary domain process (sending a confirmation email when an order is placed), updating a read model (projecting state into a query store), or cascading policy enforcement.

runs.text: Cross-context handlers:

items.text: Consume integration events from a broker, typically in a separate process or service.
Must not assume the producing context's internal model. They translate the integration event into commands or domain events in their own context using an Anti-Corruption Layer.
Must handle idempotency — the message broker may deliver the same integration event more than once. Handlers must be safe to execute multiple times without double-applying effects.
Must handle ordering issues — integration events may arrive out of order if the broker does not guarantee strict ordering. Handlers should check timestamps or version numbers before applying changes.

runs.text: Cross-context handlers that call back into the source context to fetch data defeat the purpose of asynchronous integration. If the handler cannot function on the event payload alone, the integration event payload is insufficiently rich.

An intra-context handler is a colleague who was cc'd on an email and acts immediately. A cross-context handler is a partner organization that receives a notification and must respond independently, without access to your internal systems.

cards.title: The Outbox Pattern: Reliable Event Publication
cards.teaser: Publishing events after committing a transaction still leaves a window where the process crashes between commit and publication. The outbox pattern closes that window by making event publication part of the same database transaction as the state change.

runs.text: The "collect on aggregate, publish post-commit" pattern is safe against premature publication but not against process crashes. If the service crashes after committing the database transaction but before publishing the events to the broker, those events are lost. The state changed, but no one was told.
The outbox pattern solves this with two components:

items.text: Outbox table.

An "outbox" table lives in the same database as the domain model. During the business transaction, events are inserted into the outbox table as rows. Both the aggregate state change and the event row are committed atomically — one transaction, no gap.
Relay process.

A separate background process (relay/dispatcher) reads unpublished rows from the outbox table and forwards them to the message broker. After the broker acknowledges delivery, the row is marked as published. If the relay crashes, it simply restarts from the last unacknowledged row.

runs.text: The pattern guarantees
at-least-once delivery

: in rare scenarios, an event may be delivered more than once (if the relay publishes but crashes before marking the row). Consumers must therefore be idempotent. This trade-off — at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers — is the standard in reliable messaging.

This pattern is treated in depth in Microservices Patterns ch06 (Sam Newman / Chris Richardson). The core insight: you cannot atomically commit a database write and publish to an external system. The outbox makes the external publish eventual but guaranteed.

The outbox is like a physical outbox tray on a desk: you put a letter in the tray at the same time you file the record. A mail runner periodically picks up letters and sends them. Even if the mail runner crashes, the letter is still in the tray when they restart.

cards.title: Events as Integration Contracts: Published Language Across Contexts
cards.teaser: When integration events cross bounded context boundaries they become part of the published language — a shared vocabulary that upstream and downstream contexts agree on. This makes event schema as much a contract artifact as a REST API, subject to the same versioning discipline.

runs.text: Evans identifies "Published Language" as one of the context map relationship patterns: a context makes a portion of its model available as a stable, documented schema for other contexts to consume. Integration events are the primary vehicle for Published Language in asynchronous systems.
What makes integration events a contract:

items.text: Schema definition.
The event's field names, types, required/optional status, and enum values are explicitly specified — usually in Avro, JSON Schema, or Protobuf. Consuming contexts depend on this schema.
Change management.

Because consumers have taken a dependency on the schema, breaking changes require coordination — or versioning. A field removal or type change that would be trivial inside a bounded context becomes a potentially cross-team coordination event.
Ownership.

The publishing context owns the schema. It must maintain backward compatibility or provide migration paths for consumers. The consumer cannot dictate how the schema evolves — they consume it as-is or adapt through an Anti-Corruption Layer.

runs.text: Distinguishing published language from internal model:

items.text: The internal domain event is free to use the context's full rich model.
The integration event translation layer selects a stable, consumer-appropriate subset.
Never expose internal identifiers, internal status enums, or fields that are subject to internal refactoring in integration events.

runs.text: An integration event's schema is a public API. Once other teams depend on it, you owe them backward compatibility or a migration path. Treat it like a REST endpoint contract, not like an internal function signature.

cards.title: Event Versioning: Schema Evolution
cards.teaser: Integration event schemas evolve as the business changes. Adding a field is safe. Removing one is not. Renaming is a breaking change disguised as a refactoring. Managing schema evolution without breaking consumers is one of the less glamorous and most critical skills in event-driven systems.

runs.text: Schema evolution strategies fall into two categories: backward-compatible changes and breaking changes. The goal is to maximize the former and have a disciplined process for the latter.
Safe (backward-compatible) changes:

items.text: Adding a new optional field.
Old consumers ignore the new field. New consumers use it if present. This is the workhorse of schema evolution.
Adding a new event type.
Old consumers that do not handle the new type simply skip it.
Widening a field's type
(e.g., int → long) if all consumers can handle the larger type.

runs.text: Breaking changes that require versioning:

items.text: Removing a field.
Consumers that depend on it break silently or throw. Deploy a migration plan: deprecate the field, confirm all consumers have migrated, then remove.
Renaming a field.
Equivalent to removing the old field and adding a new one. Use the expand-and-contract pattern: add the new name, deprecate the old, remove after consumers migrate.
Changing semantics without changing shape.
The most dangerous: the field name stays the same but its meaning changes. Always bump the version; never silently change meaning.

runs.text: Versioning approaches:

items.text: Topic/channel versioning:
publish v1 events and v2 events to separate topics. Consumers migrate topic by topic.
Envelope versioning:
embed a schemaVersion field in every event. Consumers read the version and branch accordingly.
Schema registry:
use a central schema registry (e.g., Confluent Schema Registry) to enforce compatibility rules at publish time.

runs.text: Adding fields to an event is safe — you're giving consumers more information and they can ignore what they don't use. Removing or renaming fields is dangerous because consumers who depend on them break the moment you deploy. Treat field removal like a database column drop: announce it, wait, then remove.

cards.title: Event-Driven Architecture: DDD's Natural Pairing
cards.teaser: Event-driven architecture and DDD fit together because bounded contexts communicate naturally through published events rather than direct API calls. Events reduce coupling between contexts, align with the domain's own language about what happened, and make system behavior traceable through an audit trail of facts.

runs.text: DDD's emphasis on bounded context autonomy and explicit integration contracts maps directly to the event-driven architectural style. A context that publishes events is self-governing: it does not need to know who is listening, what they will do, or when they will respond.
The benefits of pairing DDD with EDA:

items.text: Loose coupling.
Contexts do not take compile-time or runtime dependencies on each other's APIs. They share only the event schema — the published language.
Temporal decoupling.
The publishing context and consuming context do not need to be running simultaneously. The broker buffers events. Contexts can be independently deployed, scaled, and restarted.
Natural audit log.
Every significant business state transition produces an event. The event stream becomes a chronological history of what the system did and why — directly legible in ubiquitous language.
Reactive domain model.
Bounded contexts can react to events from other contexts without tight integration. The order context can react to a PaymentFailed event from the payments context without calling a payment API.

runs.text: The trade-offs that must be accepted:

items.text: Eventual consistency.
Asynchronous events mean the system is temporarily inconsistent between publication and handling. Business workflows must be designed to tolerate this.
Harder debugging.
Tracing a business operation across multiple contexts requires distributed tracing with correlation IDs threaded through events.

runs.text: DDD and event-driven architecture fit together because both favor autonomous pieces that communicate by broadcasting what happened rather than calling each other directly. It is the difference between a newspaper and a phone call — the paper goes out, and readers decide what to do with it.

cards.title: Event Sourcing: Events as Primary State
cards.teaser: Event sourcing takes domain events to their logical conclusion: instead of storing the current state of an aggregate, you store the sequence of events that produced that state. Current state is a projection. This fundamentally changes how aggregates are persisted, versioned, and debugged.

runs.text: In the event publication patterns discussed so far, events are a side effect — the aggregate updates its state in a relational or document store, and events are emitted as notifications. Event sourcing inverts this:
the event stream is the store
. Current state is derived by replaying the event stream from the beginning (or from a snapshot).

items.text: Append-only event log.
Every aggregate operation produces one or more events appended to an immutable log. No row is ever updated or deleted.
State reconstruction.
To load an aggregate, the application reads its event stream and applies each event to an empty aggregate instance in sequence. The final state is the result of the fold.
Complete audit trail.
Every state change is preserved forever. You can replay to any point in time, diagnose historical bugs, and derive new projections retroactively.
Temporal queries.
"What did the order look like at 2:00 PM yesterday?" — trivial with event sourcing, impossible with last-write-wins persistence.

runs.text: Event sourcing's costs:

items.text: Eventual consistency by default — read models (projections) must be rebuilt asynchronously.
Event schema evolution is harder — you cannot update past events, only apply upcasters during replay.
Long event streams require snapshots to keep load times acceptable.

runs.text: Event sourcing is covered in depth in Microservices Patterns ch09. The pattern is powerful but non-trivial — Vernon recommends applying it only where the full audit trail, temporal query capability, or CQRS/projection flexibility justifies the complexity cost.

Normal persistence stores the current snapshot: here is what the record looks like now. Event sourcing stores the history: here is every change that was ever made. The current state is what you get when you fast-forward through the entire history.
